docs.title: Muscle physiology textbook (excerpt)
docs.text: Slow-twitch (Type I) fibers develop the highest peak force and contract most rapidly, but they fatigue quickly under sustained load. Fast-twitch (Type II) fibers are, by contrast, the fatigue-resistant, aerobic fibers that sustain long-duration effort at submaximal intensity.

docs.title: Sports science survey
docs.text: Muscle biopsies of elite marathon runners average roughly 70% fast-twitch fibers in the vastus lateralis, consistent with the demands of prolonged endurance racing.

docs.title: Strength coach's notes
docs.text: We bias training toward slow-twitch recruitment for the explosive lifts — that is where peak power comes from — and lean on fast-twitch fibers during long conditioning blocks, since they resist fatigue over time.

docs.title: Fiber-type trainability review A
docs.text: Fiber-type proportions are set largely by genetics and change little with training. You can enlarge a fiber, but converting one fiber type into another is not something training reliably achieves.

docs.title: Fiber-type trainability review B
docs.text: Sustained endurance and resistance training can substantially shift fiber-type distribution over months. Type is malleable, not fixed; the proportions an athlete is born with are not the proportions they keep.

docs.title: 5 gym myths, busted
docs.text: Myth 2: fast-twitch fibers are your power-and-speed fibers and slow-twitch are the endurance ones. That basic split is the first thing every lifter should learn.
